en: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara.
First of all, one should cultivate the state of a Lord of Yoga who abides in the four sublime abodes.
[2] Thereafter, one should generate the ego-conception of the five aggregates.
Vairocana is in the aggregate of form; Vajrasūrya is in the aggregate of feeling; Padmanarteśvara is in the aggregate of perception.
In the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is Vajrarāja;
in the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is Vajrasattva;
and in the state of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Herukavajra.
The vajra of delusion is in the eyes;
the vajra of hatred is in the ears;
the vajra of envy is in the nostrils.
In speech is Passion-Vajra;
in touch is Avarice-Vajra;
in all sense bases is Sovereignty-Vajra.
The earth element is that which causes falling;
the water element is that which kills;
the fire element is that which attracts.
The wind element is Narteśvarī;
the space element is Padmajvālinī.
In this way, there is the purification of the deities within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
Then, one should visualize the vajra-fence.
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! One should place [the mantra] in the directions beginning with the east.
(b) Above that, with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should preside over a ground consisting of a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) as a lattice-work of arrows;
and through the illumination of its rays, a vajra-fence and a vajra-canopy [should be established].

(c) Oṃ gha 2 ghāṭaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ! Kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ 3! Vajrakīla, the Holder of the Vajra commands: nail down the vajra of body, speech, and mind of all obstructors! Hūṃ phaṭ! This is the mantra for nailing down.
Oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīla ākoṭaya hūṃ phaṭ | This is the mantra for striking.

[4] Then, one should visualize a moon disc at one's own heart by means of the syllable ĀḤ, and upon that, the syllable HŪṂ emitting various rays of light. Through its radiance, having seen the Guru, the Perfect Buddhas, and the others before oneself, one should worship them, prostrate, and ask for their forgiveness. Thereafter, one should go for refuge to the Three Jewels.
[5] Then: *Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.* Again, one should contemplate emptiness and abide in mind-only (*cittamātra*);
through the cultivation of the accumulations for enlightenment, knowledge is a mere appearance. || 1 ||
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.

[6] (a) Then, having awakened and visualized the mandala of the support and the supported situated within the Bhairambha and other winds; [one visualizes] the wind-mandala, transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*, marked with a banner, bow-shaped, and blue in color. Above that, the fire-mandala, transformed from the syllable *raṃ*, red in color, triangular, and marked with flames. Above that, the water-mandala, transformed from the syllable *vaṃ*, circular, white in color, and marked with a vase.

Above that is a square yellow earth mandala produced from the syllable *laṃ*, marked with three-pronged vajras at its four corners. Above that is Mount Sumeru, produced from the syllable *suṃ*, square, composed of the four jewels, and adorned with eight peaks. Above that is a double vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Above that is a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) produced from the syllable *paṃ*, having eight petals and provided with a pericarp and filaments.
(b) In the center of that is the union of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*).
[7] (a) In the center of that, one should visualize the syllable HŪṂ, which has the nature of Vajrasattva and is emitting various rays of light.
That [syllable] transforms into Śrī Heruka-vajra, situated in the center of the sun, endowed with the maṇḍala circle, and adorned with the eight perfected cremation grounds.
(b) Now, the cremation grounds are described.
In the directions, with the left and right hands, four [vajras] each should be placed in the directions starting from Īśāna, within the diamond-fence.
Caṇḍogragahvara, Jvālākulakaraṅkaka, and Vibhīṣaṇa are situated to the left in the directions starting from the east. (2)
In the northeast is Aṭṭaṭṭahāsa, Lakṣmīvana, and Hutāśana;
in the southwest is Ghorāndhakāra, and in the northwest is Kilikilārava. (3)
The cremation grounds within the vajra-enclosure are of terrifying form, filled with hosts of vetālas and bhūtas and the howling of jackals.
In this sequence, here in the eight cremation grounds, stand the trees, the guardians of the directions, the lords of the nāgas, and the lords of the clouds.
The śirīṣa, aśvattha, kaṅkeli, and cāta trees are as before;
likewise the vaṭa, karañja, and the lordly parkaṭi creeper. || 4 ||
Indra, the giver of wealth, the lord of the nāgas, and then Yama as the sovereign;
Īśāna, the consumer of oblations (Agni), the lord of the rākṣasas, and the lord of the winds (Vāyu). || 5 ||
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma,
Mahāpadma, Huluhulu, Kulika, and Śaṅkhapālaka.
Garjita, Ghūrṇita, Ghora, Āvartaghana,
Pūraṇa, Varṣaṇa, and Caṇḍa— these are the lords of the clouds.

(c) Having reflected thus upon the Blessed One as four-faced—black, dark-blue, red, and fair-complexioned; three-eyed and twelve-armed; standing in the *ālīḍha* posture; treading upon Mahābhairava and Kālarātri; embraced by Vajravārāhī; holding a vajra and a bell with the two arms engaged in embrace; wearing an elephant hide as a garment with the other two arms; a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) in the third right hand; an axe in the fourth; and a flaying knife (*kartri*) in the fifth.

In the sixth [hand], he holds a raised trident; in the third left arm, a *khaṭvāṅga* marked with a vajra; in the fourth, a skull-cup filled with blood; in the fifth, a vajra-noose; and in the sixth, the head of Brahmā. He is adorned with a crown of matted locks, his crest is decorated with a garland of skulls, and he wears a crescent moon. His head is surmounted by a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*). His face is distorted, and he is terrifying with prominent fangs. He is imbued with the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), wears a tiger-skin garment, and bears a garland of fresh human heads.

Adorned with a necklace, a breast-ornament, earrings, and a crest-jewel; adorned with the six mudrās consisting of the sacred thread and ashes; and sealed by the six mudrās through the purification of the six perfections (pāramitās).

(d) In front of him is the Blessed Lady, red in color, with one face, two arms, and three eyes; her hair is loose and she is naked, wearing a girdle adorned with fragments. With her left arm she embraces a skull-cup containing the blood of Māra and other wicked ones, while with her right [hand she holds]...
Threatening all directions with her vajra for menacing the wicked,
possessing great splendor like the fire at the end of an aeon, flowing [with blood], and fond of blood,
she is encircled by her two shanks and consists of the nature of great bliss and compassion.
Then, having wrapped [the vessel],
one should place Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī— bestowers of all accomplishments— in the positions of the directions of the lotus. 8.
Black, dark green, red, and fair-complexioned, they have one face and four arms;
in their left hands they hold a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skull-cup, and in their right hands a ḍamaru drum and a flaying knife.
Three-eyed, with disheveled hair, naked, and standing in the ālīḍha posture;
their faces are terrifying with bared fangs, and they are adorned with the five mudrās. || 10 ||
In the intermediate directions are four vessels of the thought of awakening and so forth;
they are designated as the four offerings through the purification of passion and the other afflictions, including delusion. (11)

(f) First is the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), adorned with a blue vajra-garland on its eight spokes. On its eastern spoke, at Pullīramalaya, are Khaṇḍakapālin and Pracaṇḍā; on the north, at Jālandhara, Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī; on the west, at Oḍḍiyāna, Kaṅkāla and Prabha-vatī; on the south, at Arbuda, Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin and Mahānāsā. This is the *pīṭha*. In the southeast, at Godāvarī, are Surāvairin and Vīramatī; in the southwest, at Rāmeśvara, Amitābha and Kharvarī.
In the northwest, at Devīkoṭa, is Vajraprabhā Laṅkeśvarī; in the northeast, in Mālava, is Vajradehā Drumacchāyā. This is the Upapīṭha. Thus is the Citta-cakra.

(g) The second speech-wheel is joined with a garland of red lotuses. On its eastern spoke, at Kāmarūpa, are Aṅkurikā and Airāvatī. On the north, at Oḍra, are Vajrajaṭila and Mahābhairavī; this is a *kṣetra*. On the west, at Triśakuni, are Mahāvīra and Vāyuvegā. On the south, at Kośala, are Vajrahūṃkāra and Surābhakṣī; this is an *upakṣetra*. In the southeast, at Kaliṅga, are Subhadra and Śyāmadevī. In the southwest, at Lampāka, are Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā; this is a *cchandoha*.
In Kāñcī to the northwest is Mahāvairavahayakarṇā; in Himālaya to the northeast is Virūpākṣakhagānanā. This is the Upacchandoha. Thus is the Wheel of Speech (vākcakra).

(h) The third body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) is surrounded by a row of white wheels. On its eastern spoke, in Pretapurī, is Mahābalacakravegā; on the northern [spoke], in Gṛhadevatā, is Ratnavajrakhaṇḍarohā. This is the *melāpaka*. On the western [spoke], in Saurāṣṭra, is Hayagrīvaśauṇḍinī; on the southern [spoke], in Suvarṇadvīpa, is Ākāśagarbha. (p. 7)

Cakravarmiṇī; this is the secondary meeting place (*upamelāpaka*). In the city of Āgneyī is Śrī Heruka Suvīrā; in Sindhu of Nairṛtī is Padmanarteśvara Mahābalā; this is the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). In Marudeśa of Vāyavī is Vairocana Cakravartinī; in Kulatā of Aiśānī is Vajrasattva Mahāvīryā; this is the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*). Thus is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*).
The heroes, Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, have one face and four arms;
they possess three eyes, wear crowns of matted hair, and are adorned with turbans. || 12 ||
With his two arms in embrace, he holds a vajra and a vajra-bell;
likewise, a khaṭvāṅga in his left hand and a ḍamaru drum in his right. (13)
Their bodies are adorned with the five mudrās and so forth, and they stand in the ālīḍha posture;
likewise, the goddesses beginning with Pracaṇḍā have one face and two arms. (14)
With skull-cups in their hands for embracing, and with flaying knives for threatening the wicked, they have three eyes, possess fierce forms, and are adorned with loose, disheveled hair. || 15 ||
Others, having attained the yoga of non-duality, were naked;
they wore necklaces, crest-jewels, armlets, earrings, and the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*).
With the jingling sounds of their girdles and the garlands of heads adorning their necks, [they resounded]. (16)

(i) At the eastern, northern, western, and southern gates are Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Sūkarāsyā. In the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī.
Just as it is for the host of ḍākinīs, so it is for Kākāsyā and the others according to their divisions;
likewise, the two goddesses established by the ritual rule possess two forms that are truly captivating. (17)

The fierce ones, who have abandoned delusion and are intent upon compassion for the sake of sentient beings, all possess a garland of vajras upon their foreheads, [belonging] to all the heroic yoginīs. (18)

[8] Hereafter, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are to be practiced through union with the deities. How are they so? The application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is Ḍākinī; the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is Lāmā; the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is Khaṇḍarohā; the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*) is Rūpiṇī; the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandarddhipāda*) is Pracaṇḍā; the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīryarddhipāda*) is Caṇḍākṣī; the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation (*mīmāṃsarddhipāda*) is Prabhāvatī; and the basis of psychic power consisting of mind (*cittarddhipāda*) is Mahānāsā.
The faculty of faith is Vīramatī; the faculty of energy is Kharvarī;
the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī; the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā; and the faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī.

The power of faith is Mahābhairavā; the power of vigor is Vāyuvegā; the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī; the power of concentration is Śyāmadevī; the power of wisdom is Subhadrā. The factor of enlightenment that is concentration is Hayakarṇā; the factor of enlightenment that is vigor is Khagānanā; the factor of enlightenment that is joy is Cakravegā; the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy is Khaṇḍarohā; the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena is Śauṇḍinī; the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is Cakravarmiṇī; the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is Suvīrā.

Right view is Mahābalā; right resolve is Cakravartinī; right speech is Mahāvīryā; right action is Kākāsyā; right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā; right mindfulness is Sūkarāsyā; and in right concentration resides the Blessed One, Śrī Herukavajra.

The production of unarisen wholesome states is Yamadāḍhī; the preservation of arisen wholesome states is Yamadūtī; the abandonment of arisen unwholesome states is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī; and the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states is Yamamathanī.
[9] (a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme body-maṇḍala, according to the sequence of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, through the purification of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). 19.
(b) Pūjā-ogorā-de-mākā-o-triko-kala-kāhi-pre-gṛ-sau-su-nasi-maku.

(c) At Pullīramalaya on the head is Pracaṇḍā; at Jālandhara on the crest-lock is Caṇḍākṣī; at Oḍḍiyāna on the right ear is Prabhāvatī; at Arbuda on the back of the head is Mahānāsā. This *pīṭha* is the stage of Pramuditā. At Godāvarī on the left ear is Vīramatī; at Rāmeśvara between the eyebrows is Kharvarī; at Devīkoṭa on the eyes is Laṅkeśvarī; at Mālava on both shoulders is Drumacchāyā. This *upapīṭha* is the stage of Vimalā. [These are] the *khecarīs* of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*).

(d) In Kāmarūpa, at the two armpits, is Airāvatī; in Oḍra, at the pair of breasts, is Mahābhairavā. This is the field (*kṣetra*), the Prabhākari stage. In Triśakuni, at the navel, is Vāyuvegā; in Kośala, at the tip of the nose, is Surābhakṣī. This is the secondary field (*upakṣetra*), the Arciṣmatī stage. In Kaliṅga, at the mouth, is Śyāmadevī; in Lampāka, at the throat, is Subhadrā. This is the chandoha, the Sudurjayā stage. In Kāñcī, at the heart, is Hayakarṇā; in Himālaya, at the penis, is Khagānanā.
This is the secondary chandoha (*upacchandoha*), the Abhimukhī stage. These are the Earth-Walkers (*bhūcarī*) of the wheel of speech.
(e) In Pretapurī, at the *liṅga*, is Cakravegā; in Gṛhadevatā, at the anus, is Khaṇḍarohā. This is the *melāpaka*.

The Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching) Bhūmi: at Saurāṣṭra, in the two thighs, is Śauṇḍinī; at Suvarṇadvīpa, in the two shanks, is Cakravarmiṇī; the Upamelāpaka is the Acalā (Immovable) Bhūmi. In the city, in the fingers, is Suvīrā; at Sindhū, on the tops of the feet, is Mahābalā; the cremation ground is the Sādhumatī Bhūmi. In the desert, in the two big toes, is Cakravartinī; at Kulatā, in the two knees, is Mahāvīryā; the secondary cremation ground is the Dharmameghā Bhūmi; [and] at the body-wheel is Pātālavāsinī.
[10] Through the division of body, speech, and mind, by virtue of having the nature of the three syllables,
one shall become a single form in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld in an instant.
The self whose nature is the yoga of instantaneous form, like a seal of instantaneous form, instantaneous in every respect and by all means—[one] should utter the mantra instantaneously. (21)
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all heroes and yoginīs. Oṃ, all phenomena are pure vajra; I am pure vajra.
[11] (a) Then, having understood the two armors, the yogin should visualize the wheel of gnosis; having caused it to enter the wheel of commitment by means of the mantra of the mudrās. || 22 ||

(b) Now I shall describe the two armors: OṂ HAḤ at the heart; NA MAḤ HI on the head; SVĀ HĀ HŪ at the crest-lock; VAUṢAṬ HE on the two shoulders; HŪṂ HŪṂ HOḤ on the two eyes; PHAṬ HAṂ on all limbs as the weapon-mantra.
First is Vajrasattva; in the second resides Vairocana;
in the third is Padmanarteśvara, the King; in the fourth is called Śrī Heruka;
in the fifth is Vajrasūrya, and in the sixth is Paramāśva—thus is one protected by the armor of the six. 23.
Oṃ vaṃ Vajravārāhī; hāṃ yoṃ Yāminī; hrīṃ moṃ Mohanī; hreṃ hrīṃ Sañcālinī; hūṃ hūṃ Saṃtrāsanī; phaṭ phaṭ Caṇḍikā. [This is] the weapon-mantra for all limbs.
At the navel, the heart, and likewise the mouth, as well as the head, the crest-lock, and the weapon-mantra.
[12] (a) Having indeed formed the foremost knot with the middle needle,
and having firmly pressed the two thumbs like vajras,
one should place it in the middle of the forehead region and then rotate it again in a circular motion. || 25 ||
With his feet treading [the ground] and his gaze directed upward, by the sound of the syllable *phaṃ* at his crown,
he draws forth the heroes and yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
(b) Then the heart-seal (hṛdayamudrā) should be shown: the blissful [state] of the network of ḍākinīs, whirling with the left and right hands.
[13] Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā | This is the heart mantra.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the near-heart mantra (upahṛdayamantra).
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the heart mantra.
Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the subsidiary heart mantra (upahṛdayamantra).

Oṃ kara 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kuru 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ caṇḍākṣīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bandha 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ prabhāvatīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ trāsaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahānāse hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kṣobhaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ vīramatīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hrīṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kharvarīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ hraḥ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ Laṅkeśvarīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ pheṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ Drumacchāye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ phaṭ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ Airāvatīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ daha 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ Mahābhairavīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ paca 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ Vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bhakṣa 2 vasarudhirāntramālāvalambine hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ surābhakṣīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 saptapātālagatabhujaṅgasarpaṃ vā tarjaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śyāmadevīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ākaṭṭha 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hrīṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hayakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ jñau hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kṣyāṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ hāṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hrīṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śauṇḍinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravarmiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kili 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ suvīre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ sili 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hili 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ cakravartinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ dhili 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kākāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ulūkāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ śvānāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ sūkarāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadāḍhīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadūtīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamadaṃṣṭriṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ yamamathanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ḍākinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ lāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose crown of matted hair is formidable, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose face is terrifying with fierce, gaping fangs, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him resplendent with a thousand arms, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the bearer of the uplifted axe, noose, trident, and khaṭvāṅga staff, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to the wearer of a tiger-skin garment, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, to him whose body is like a great mass of smoke and darkness, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! This is the mantra for worship.
[14] Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth, so shall I bathe you with pure, divine water. || 27 ||
Oṃ āḥ, for the glory of the commitment of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ. This is the empowerment mantra.
[15] Oṃ vajrārali hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Vajra-ḍākinīs, you are the commitment; appear, hoḥ!
At midnight, one should offer the bali with the vajrāñjali mudrā opened upwards.

Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! All you yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering; protect the samaya; grant me all accomplishments; eat, drink, and smell as much as you desire and according to your pleasure; do not transgress; be my helpers in every way for the sake of purifying true happiness—hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

[16] Khaṇḍakapālin resides in the nails and teeth; Mahākaṅkāla in the hair of the head and body; Kaṅkāla in the skin and excrement; Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin in the flesh; Surāvairin in the sinews; Amitābha in the bones; Vajraprabha in the kidneys; Vajradeha in the heart; Aṅkurika in the eyes; Vajrajaṭila in the bile; Mahāvīra in the lungs; Vajrahūṃkāra in the intestines; Subhadra in the tendons and veins; and Vajrabhadra in the stomach.

Feces is Mahābhairava; the parting of the hair is Virūpākṣa; phlegm is Mahābala; pus is Ratnavajra; blood is Hayagrīva; sweat is Ākāśagarbha; fat is Śrīheruka; tears are Padmanarteśvara; spittle is Vairocana; and nasal mucus is Vajrasattva. Such is the purification of the limbs of the heroes.
[17] That which is the Hero beginning with the root mantra is conceived as the Brahma-thread and so forth;
however, the twenty-four Heroes are conceived as the constituent elements (dhātus) within the body. || 28 ||
With six [syllables] of the armor-mantra, this mudrā is the adornment of the limbs;
with the mantra of Vajravārāhī, the necklace is the ornament for the neck. (29)
The rosary, adorned with fifty beads, belongs to the deity by means of the heart-mantra;
the earring that beautifies the ear belongs to the seven-syllable mantra.
The supreme ḍākinīs of all the Buddhas wear garments of skin;
with the mantra "ṣaḍyoginī," they have their girdles fashioned as ornaments. (31)
The mantra-drink vessel of the Yoginī of the entire wheel is the mantra called Vairocanī, which has its crest adorned with a skull-cup.
Having thus reflected upon oneself as being well-protected by the incantation of self-restraint,
one should always remain in celibacy, indeed reciting the mantra honored with eight steps.
Having reflected thus, the yogi of great intelligence, whose self is yoga and who is free from all fear, should wander within the observance of the Cakrasaṃvara.
The practice of the five colors is conceived as being of a single color;
with a mind whose nature is free from conceptual construction, enjoy the five objects of desire.
Like a lion, the yogi should wander about, entirely devoid of all apprehension. (35)
[18] Having meditated upon the vowels and consonants at the beginning through the great yoga, one should rest; one should visualize a full moon mandala situated at the base of the navel. 36.
One should contemplate the supreme syllable situated in its center;
one should visualize the form of the deity as the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind. That which transcends the mass [of syllables] shall be his; one should visualize that very mind. (37)
He should contemplate the inconceivable, yet even that mind is not perceived;
he should indeed contemplate the inconceivable, and thereby he will attain the dhāraṇī.
[19] The form of the deity is the khaṭvāṅga; the sound of the damaru is wisdom.
The Blessed One, the Hero, is said to be day, and the Yoginī is said to be night. 39.
The hero who has emerged from nirvāṇa is the sixth, created by the mind;
he is the emanation of the Pure Dharma, manifested in the form of Vārāhī.

The syllable Śrī is non-dual gnosis; the syllable Ha is the emptiness of causes and so forth; the syllable Ru is the array that has transcended [all things]; and the syllable Ka does not abide anywhere. (41)
The yogi’s mind finds rest, yet nirvāṇa is not shown;
at the time of death for yogis, however, there appear the heroes and yoginīs, such as Śrī Heruka. 42.
With hands busy with various flowers, bearing various banners and flags,
accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments and various offerings of transcendence,
this conceptualization called "death" is led to the state of the Sky-farer (khecarī). 43.
Thus, by these very words of Śrī Lūyī— who have uprooted the two extremes through familiarity with the lineage of oral tradition (*āmnāya-paramparā*),
who delight in the kingdom of the non-dual Dharma, and who seek this [truth]—
other tantras are drawn forth.
This very realization of the fierce, magnificent Saṃvara has thus been set forth.
The *Śrīcakrasaṃvarābhisamaya* composed by the venerable Lūyīpāda is completed.
